pysbd: As several US states consider religious freedom laws, which opponents suggest may open the door to discrimination against gay and lesbian customers, Walmart has emerged as a bellwether for shifting public opinion on this contentious issue.

Walmart's staunch criticism of a religious freedom law in its home state of Arkansas, came after the company had already said it would increase pay for about 500,000 workers well above the federal minimum wage.
Observers are suggesting that the Republican Party should take notice of the stand that Walmart has taken.

Former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty, told CNN that Walmart's actions "foreshadow where the Republican Party will need to move." "The Republican Party will have to better stand for" ideas on helping the middle class, said Pawlenty, the head of the Financial Services Roundtable, a Washington lobbying group for the finance industry.

The party's leaders must be "willing to put forward ideas that will help modest income workers, such as a reasonable increase in the minimum wage, and prohibit discrimination in things such as jobs, housing, public accommodation against gays and lesbians."

Benaud was inducted into the Sport Australia Hall of Fame in 1985 and had a successful 64 Test matches.
Benaud was not only popular in Australia, but also in the UK where he spent over four decades with the BBC, taking the sport into millions of British living rooms.
Australian Prime Minister, Tony Abbott, said in a written statement “To most Australians Richie Benaud was cricket. He personified its traditions and its values.”
Benaud led the Australian side from 1958/59 through to 1963/1964, never losing a series in his 28 Tests as captain.
Benaud was the first cricketer to reach a Test double of 2,000 runs and 200 wickets.
